title: New NPS Rules and Tax Benefits
summary: NPS tax deductions under sections 123 and 124, what changed on 16 December 2025, withdrawal rules by subscriber type, tax at exit and how UPS differs.
body_markdown:
NPS, the National Pension System, is a retirement account regulated by PFRDA (the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority) and invested in shares and bonds. Two things have changed. Since 16 December 2025 a subscriber who is not a government employee can take up to 80% of the balance as cash at a normal exit, against 60% before. But the tax exemption still stops at 60%. And the deductions now sit in sections 123 and 124 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, not in 80C and 80CCD.


## What tax benefits does NPS give?


NPS gives three tax deductions: two for your own money, old regime only, and one for your employer's money. The old regime is the one you choose instead of the default. A deduction is an amount you subtract from your income before tax is worked out.


Your own contribution counts under section 123 (the old Section 80C), inside the ₹1,50,000 limit it shares with its other items. The extra ₹50,000 sits over and above that limit.


Old section Section in the 2025 Act What it covers Works in the new regime?


80CCD(1) 123 (Schedule XV para 1(y)) Your own contribution: up to 10% of salary if you are an employee, or 20% of gross total income (your income before these deductions) for others, inside the ₹1,50,000 No


80CCD(1B) 124(3) Up to ₹50,000 more, over and above the ₹1,50,000 No


80CCD(2) 124(1) Your employer's contribution: up to 14% of salary if the employer is the Central or a State Government, 10% for other employers Yes


The same amount cannot be claimed twice. The[deductions guide](https://koshex.com/blog/deductions-under-section-80c-80ccc-80ccd-and-80d) lists the other section 123 items.


## Which NPS deductions work in the new tax regime?


Only your employer's contribution, under section 124(1) (the old 80CCD(2)), works in the new tax regime. The new regime is the default one and allows almost no deductions, so your own contributions are old regime only.


The employer's limit differs by regime. Under the old regime it is 14% of salary for a Central or State Government employer and 10% for any other employer. Under the new regime it is 14% for every employer. Salary here counts dearness allowance when your terms of employment include it.


There is a ceiling on the employer side. If your employer's contributions to your EPF, NPS and superannuation together pass ₹7,50,000 in a year, the excess is a perquisite: a benefit taxed as part of your salary.


Here is what the extra ₹50,000 saves, under the old regime only. Assume you are under 60 and your total income is at or below ₹50 lakh, so no surcharge applies.


- If your income was already above ₹10,00,000 before the deduction and still is after it, the ₹50,000 saves ₹15,000 at the 30% slab plus ₹600 cess, or ₹15,600. Cess is an extra 4% charge on the tax.
- If your income was at most ₹10,00,000 before the deduction and is above ₹5,00,000 after it, the ₹50,000 saves ₹10,000 at the 20% slab plus ₹400 cess, or ₹10,400.


The[new tax regime guide](https://koshex.com/blog/features-of-the-new-tax-regime-and-its-benefits) compares the regimes.


## What changed in the NPS rules in December 2025?


From 16 December 2025, a non-government subscriber's normal exit is at 15 years of subscription or age 60, whichever comes first. Up to 80% can then be taken as cash, with at least 20% buying an annuity. A normal exit is closing the account once you reach that point, and you can put it off until 85. An annuity is a regular pension bought with part of your balance.


Before 16 December 2025 it was 60% lump sum and 40% annuity. A lump sum is the cash part, taken in one go. Here is what moved:


- **Cash and annuity.** Up to 80% as cash and at least 20% to an annuity, for subscribers who are not government employees. Government subscribers keep the 40% annuity rule.
- **Small balances.** A balance of ₹8 lakh or less can be withdrawn in full. Between ₹8 lakh and ₹12 lakh, up to ₹6 lakh can be taken as cash. These bands now apply to government subscribers too.
- **Staying on.** You can defer exit and the annuity purchase to age 85.
- **Early exit.** A premature exit, which is closing the account before the normal exit point, needs at least 80% in an annuity. All Citizen subscribers (those who join on their own, not through an employer) have no minimum period before they can leave. A balance of ₹5 lakh or less can be withdrawn in full.
- **Partial withdrawals.** Skill development and start-ups are no longer purposes. Repaying a loan against the account is.
- **Loans.** PFRDA's rules now let a regulated lender lend against up to 25% of your own contributions; PFRDA has said separate guidelines will follow.


## When can you withdraw money from NPS?


You can take money out in three ways. One is a normal exit. Another is an earlier premature exit, with most of it buying an annuity. The third is a partial withdrawal after three years, for a listed purpose. Which rule applies depends on whether you work for the government.


### If you are not a government employee


This covers the All Citizen and corporate models. At a normal exit at least 20% of the corpus, the total balance in the account, must buy an annuity. Up to 80% can come out as cash or through systematic withdrawal, explained below.


On the small-balance bands, a corpus of ₹7,50,000 can be withdrawn in full. On ₹10,00,000, up to ₹6,00,000 can be taken as cash. The other ₹4,00,000 must either buy an annuity or be drawn over at least six years through systematic unit redemption. That means selling a fixed number of units at regular intervals.


Take Arvind, 52, a private-sector employee in Chennai who opened his account at 37. He has completed 15 years of subscription, so leaving now is a normal exit even though he is under 60. His corpus is ₹30,00,000. At least ₹6,00,000 must buy an annuity, and up to ₹24,00,000 can come out as cash, at once or in instalments.


Had he left before 15 years and before 60, that would be a premature exit, and at least ₹24,00,000 (80%) would have to buy an annuity.


### If you are a government employee


For government employees the 40% annuity rule stays. At retirement at least 40% of the NPS balance must buy a pension, and up to 60% can be taken as cash, in one go or in instalments.


A balance of ₹8 lakh or less can be taken out in full, and between ₹8 lakh and ₹12 lakh up to ₹6 lakh can be taken as cash. If a government employee leaves early through permitted resignation, dismissal or removal, at least 80% must buy a pension unless the balance is ₹5 lakh or less.


On the same ₹30,00,000, a government subscriber at retirement must put at least ₹12,00,000 into an annuity, and up to ₹18,00,000 can come out as cash.


### Partial withdrawals


A partial withdrawal is taking some money out while the account stays open. After three years in NPS you can take out up to 25% of your own contributions, not counting returns, for a listed purpose. Each withdrawal is capped at that 25%, and an unused part stays available next time.


The purposes are:


- Higher education of your children.
- Marriage of your children.
- Buying or building a house, once, in your own name or jointly with your spouse, if you do not already own one other than an ancestral house.
- Medical treatment or hospitalisation of you, your spouse, children or parents.
- Expenses from your disability or incapacitation.
- Settling a loan taken from a regulated lender against a lien on your pension account.


Before 60 you can do this up to four times, at least four years apart. After 60 you can do it any number of times until 85, with a gap of at least three years between withdrawals.


NPS Trust's FAQ says you can start one by logging in to your pension account or by submitting a physical form to your service provider (called a PoP).


For an employee, the amount withdrawn this way is not taxed. Under the Income-tax Act, 2025 the exclusion is capped at 25% of the contributions the employee made. The same applies to a parent or guardian withdrawing from a minor's account.


### Taking the cash part in instalments


At exit you do not have to take the cash part in one go. You can draw it as a fixed amount at regular intervals, or by selling a fixed number of units each time, while the rest stays invested. These are called systematic lump sum withdrawal and systematic unit redemption.


### What happens to the money if the subscriber dies?


If a subscriber in the All Citizen or corporate model dies, the nominee gets the whole balance. A nominee is the person you name to receive the money. Nomination is mandatory, and you can name up to three nominees. The nominee may take it as cash, in instalments or as a pension. What the nominee receives on the subscriber's death is not taxed as the nominee's income.


For government employees who die in service, at least 80% buys a pension for the family unless the balance is ₹8 lakh or less.


## How is NPS money taxed when you take it out?


Up to 60% of what you are paid at exit is tax-free. If you take more than 60% as cash, which the rules now allow, the part above 60% is added to your income for that year and taxed at your slab rate. The slab rate is the rate for the income slab your total income falls in.


The amount used to buy a pension is not taxed when you buy it. The pension itself is taxed as income when you receive it.


Back to Arvind. Sixty per cent is ₹18,00,000. If he takes the full ₹24,00,000 as cash, ₹18,00,000 is tax-free and the other ₹6,00,000 is added to his income for the year. The ₹6,00,000 used for the annuity is not income that year, but each year's pension is. If he takes ₹18,00,000 as cash, none of it is taxed.


How an annuity is chosen and taxed year by year is in the[annuity guide](https://koshex.com/blog/nps-annuity-and-pension-plans) . For what to do with the cash, see[retirement income](https://koshex.com/blog/retirement-income) .


## How is UPS different from NPS for government employees?


UPS, the Unified Pension Scheme, pays a pension worked out from your pay and years of service, not from what an account has built up. It has been an option inside NPS for Central Government employees since 1 April 2025.


With 25 years of qualifying service, UPS pays 50% of your average basic pay over the last 12 months. It pays less for 10 to 25 years, and at least ₹10,000 a month after 10 years. Your spouse gets 60% of it after you.


You put in 10% of basic pay plus dearness allowance, as in NPS, and the Government matches it; both go into your individual corpus.


Existing staff had until 30 November 2025 to choose UPS, and new joiners have 30 days. Without an option, the employee continues under NPS.


Since 23 December 2025, a UPS member can switch back to NPS once, no later than 12 months before retirement, or at resignation, but not on dismissal or removal. On switching, the NPS exit rules apply and the UPS payouts are lost.


UPS also pays a lump sum of one-tenth of last basic pay plus dearness allowance for every completed six months of service. At retirement, up to 60% of the individual corpus and that lump sum are tax-free. The[NPS account guide](https://koshex.com/blog/national-pension-scheme-nps-how-to-open-nps-account) covers opening an account, and the[NPS calculator](https://koshex.com/calculators/nps-calculator) shows how a corpus can build up.
